checks.claim: Key: a skater who shoves a wall rolls backward, away from it, because the wall pushes back on her
checks.note: OpenStax: 'When you push on a wall, the wall pushes back on you.' Alloprof (https://www.alloprof.qc.ca/en/students/vl/physics/newton-s-third-law-of-motion-p1090): a person on a skateboard who pushes the wall 'will move away from it, because the wall has exerted a force on him.'

checks.claim: Wrong: 'She stays put, since a wall cannot push' (a still wall does push back)
checks.note: Truly wrong: the wall pushes back on her. Not defensible.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'She stays put, since the wall did not move'
checks.note: Truly wrong: the wall's push acts on her, not on the wall; on skates with a hard shove she rolls away.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'She rolls forward, carried by her own push'
checks.note: Truly wrong: her push acts on the wall; the force on her points away from the wall. Objects do not carry stored force.

checks.claim: Context: the wall pushes back just as hard, at the same moment; still things push back; force is not stored
checks.note: WHRO: force pairs 'Act at the same time'; 'The very instant that you start to push against the wall is the exact instant that the wall starts to push against you.' Context does not pair the normal force with weight.

checks.claim: Key: the water pushes forward on her hands (she pushes water back, water pushes her forward)
checks.note: Grokipedia: a swimmer pushes backward against the water and the water pushes the swimmer forward. Alloprof: a swimmer 'must exert a thrust with his arms and legs in the opposite sense.' Naming only the hands is a fair simplification for a stem about arm strokes.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The water, closing in behind her body'
checks.note: Truly wrong: water closing in behind a body does not propel a swimmer; the forward push is the water's reaction to her strokes.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The force she stores up with each stroke'
checks.note: Truly wrong: 'Objects don't contain force'; a force is an interaction that lasts only while it acts. (Her glide between strokes is inertia, not a stored force; the choice is still wrong.)

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The air above, pressing on her back'
checks.note: Truly wrong: air pressure on her back presses down, not forward, and is not what propels a swimmer.

checks.claim: Context: hands and arms push water back, water pushes them forward just as hard; no stored force; air does not push her along
checks.note: All true at grade level.

checks.claim: Key: in empty space a firing rocket speeds up, pushed forward by its exhaust gas
checks.note: NASA Glenn: 'The rocket pushes on the gas, and the gas in turn pushes on the rocket.' Grokipedia Newton's laws: the engine expels exhaust backward and the gases push the rocket forward. (A pedant could note a craft drifting tail-first would slow, but the stem's 'out of the back' plus the wrong choice's reason 'held back by the gas' keep the key unique.)

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It stays put, with no air to push against'
checks.note: OpenStax: 'It is a common misconception that rockets propel themselves by pushing on the ground or on the air behind them.' Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It slows down, held back by the gas'
checks.note: Truly wrong: the gas pushes the rocket forward, not back.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'It drifts backward, along with the gas'
checks.note: Truly wrong: the rocket moves the opposite way to its exhaust.

checks.claim: Context: a rocket never needs air and works even better in empty space, where its exhaust escapes freely
checks.note: NASA Glenn: 'rockets actually work better in space than they do in air'; 'In space, the exhaust gases can escape freely.' OpenStax agrees ('work better in a vacuum').

checks.claim: Context: a New York Times editorial mocked Goddard on this point in 1920
checks.note: Unsigned 'Topics of the Times' editorial, 13 January 1920, said a rocket needs 'something better than a vacuum against which to react'. Not quoted in the context, so no quotation check needed.

checks.claim: Context: the paper printed a correction in July 1969, during the flight of Apollo 11
checks.note: The correction ran 17 July 1969, the day after launch (Grokipedia also gives 20 July in one place; both dates fall within the flight). NASA: Apollo 11 launched 16 July 1969, splashed down 24 July 1969. Secondary reports (Popular Science, https://www.popsci.com/military-aviation-amp-space/article/2009-07/new-york-times-nasa-youre-right-rockets-do-work-space) agree on 17 July.

checks.claim: Key: with the neck pointing down, the released balloon shoots up, pushed by the air rushing out
checks.note: NASA Glenn: 'Air inside a balloon is compressed by the balloon's rubber walls'; 'When the nozzle is released, air escapes through it and the balloon is propelled in the opposite direction.' A real balloon soon zigzags, but its first motion is away from the jet, so 'shoots up' holds.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Drops down, dragged by the air rushing out'
checks.note: Truly wrong: the escaping air pushes the balloon the opposite way to the jet. (An empty balloon does fall at the end, but not 'dragged by the air rushing out'; the choice's reason is false.)

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Floats up, since the air inside is light' (the brief's partly-true worry)
checks.note: Truly wrong. The balloon does go up, but the stem asks why, and the reason is false: 'a balloon that you fill up with your own breath will not float' (Children's Museum of Atlanta). Breath is mostly nitrogen and oxygen plus 4 to 5 percent carbon dioxide (Scientific American, https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/how-heavy-is-your-air/), and the air inside is slightly squeezed, so it is not lighter than the room's air; the rubber adds weight. 'Air is light' in the everyday sense does not make the choice right, because it does not make the balloon float. Key and this choice are distinct in their reasons ('shoots up, pushed' vs 'floats up, light').

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Stays put, since air is too light to push'
checks.note: Truly wrong: escaping air does propel the balloon.

checks.claim: Context: breath is not lighter than room air, so a breath-filled balloon does not float; a lighter-than-air gas such as helium is needed
checks.note: Children's Museum of Atlanta: breath balloon 'will not float'; helium is one of the 'very light' gases. Illinois Physics Van (https://van.physics.illinois.edu/ask/listing/2129): a helium balloon floats because of its lower density. (Fresh, warm, humid breath is a hair lighter for a moment, but once in the balloon at room temperature and slightly compressed it is no lighter; fine at grade level.)

checks.claim: Key: the bug pushes on the truck just as hard as the truck pushes on the bug
checks.note: Third law (OpenStax; NGSS PS2.A 'equal in strength', https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/ms-ps2-1-motion-and-stability-forces-and-interactions). Physics Classroom's bug-and-bus exercise and a Swarthmore worksheet (https://www.sccs.swarthmore.edu/users/09/azelask1/pdfs/3dforce_exsol.pdf) give equal forces on bug and windshield.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Far more weakly than the truck pushes on it'
checks.note: Truly wrong: the forces are equal (the 'greater mass implies greater force' misconception, https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.00967).

checks.claim: Wrong: 'A bit more weakly than the truck pushes on it'
checks.note: Truly wrong: exactly equal, not slightly less.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Not at all, since the bug is far too light'
checks.note: Truly wrong: every interaction gives a pair; the bug pushes on the truck.

checks.claim: Context: the same-sized push changes the light bug's motion enormously and the heavy truck's hardly at all, which is why only the bug is squashed
checks.note: Same force, small mass gives big acceleration (NASA cannon example; Florida SC.5.P.13.3, https://www.cpalms.org/PreviewStandard/PrintStandard/1740). The standard classroom explanation of the splat is the bug's huge sudden change of motion. Strictly, the windshield also survives because glass is strong and the bug is soft; if the writer wants it airtight, 'and the soft little bug is crushed while the strong glass holds' could be added. Not an error at grade level.

checks.claim: Key: the bat's push and the ball's push do not cancel because each acts on a different object
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'These forces act on different bodies and thus do not cancel each other out within a single body.' OpenStax: they 'do not act on the same body. Thus, they do not cancel each other.'

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The bat pushes harder than the ball does'
checks.note: Truly wrong: the pair is equal in strength.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The ball pushes back a moment later'
checks.note: Truly wrong: TEKS 6.7C 'simultaneous force pairs'; Grokipedia Reaction (physics): reaction forces are 'simultaneous'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Forces pointing opposite ways never cancel'
checks.note: Truly wrong: equal, opposite forces on the same object do cancel (zero net force, no change in motion), as in a balanced tug-of-war.

checks.claim: Context: equal, opposite, same moment; forces cancel only on the same object, as two equal pulls on one rope do; the ball's push acts on the bat
checks.note: All true. The rope example is balanced forces on one object, correctly told; no normal-force/weight pairing appears.

checks.claim: Stem: Isaac Newton's third law says forces always come in pairs
checks.note: Third law from Newton's Principia (1687): 'To every action there is always opposed an equal reaction.'

checks.claim: Key: the partner of the hammer's push on the nail is the nail's push up on the hammer
checks.note: A third-law pair is the same two bodies acting on each other ('the mutual actions of two bodies upon each other'). Hammer pushes down on nail, so nail pushes up on hammer. Pearson's worked answer (https://www.pearson.com/channels/physics/asset/47121665/when-a-hammer-strikes-a-nail-and-drives-it-in) agrees.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The board's push up on the nail'
checks.note: Truly wrong: it acts on the same object (the nail) and involves a third body, so it belongs to the nail-board pair. This is the same trap as normal force vs weight, and the question gets it right: WHRO says the table's push on the book and the book's weight are 'not a pair of Newton's Third Law forces'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The hand's push down on the hammer'
checks.note: Truly wrong: a hand-hammer interaction, a different pair.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Earth's pull down on the nail'
checks.note: Truly wrong: its partner is the nail's pull on Earth (as in Wikipedia's book example, where the reaction to Earth's pull is 'the gravitational pull of the book acting on the Earth').

checks.claim: Context: a pair is the same two objects; the board's push is another force on the nail, in the nail-board pair
checks.note: True; does not repeat Grokipedia's normal-force/weight error.

checks.claim: Key: Earth is so massive it barely moves toward the falling apple
checks.note: Grokipedia Reaction (physics): Earth pulls the apple down and the apple pulls Earth up equally; Earth's acceleration is 'on the order of 10^-24 m/s²', 'imperceptible but nonetheless real'. OpenStax: a boy pulled down by Earth 'pulls upward on Earth'. (This sentence of that Grokipedia page is sound; its normal-force line is the faulty one, and it is not used.)

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The apple's pull on Earth is far weaker'
checks.note: Truly wrong: the gravitational pair is equal (w and -w).

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The two pulls cancel each other out'
checks.note: Truly wrong: they act on different bodies, so they do not cancel.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'Earth's spin holds it firmly in place'
checks.note: Truly wrong: Earth's spin plays no part in why Earth's motion toward the apple is unnoticeable; mass is the reason. Not defensible.

checks.claim: Context: equal pulls; Earth's far larger mass means it moves too little to notice; the pulls act on different objects so cannot cancel; spin irrelevant
checks.note: All true. The apple is told as an ordinary falling apple, not as the Newton legend, so no myth issue.

unit_notes: All 8 questions checked on the web; no errors. The normal-force/weight error on Grokipedia's Reaction (physics) page ('this normal force forms an action-reaction pair with the gravitational force') is not repeated anywhere: the hammer-and-nail question treats the board's push on the nail as a separate pair, the bat-and-ball context's rope example is correctly told as balanced forces on one object, and the apple question pairs Earth's pull on the apple with the apple's pull on Earth. Two soft notes, neither an error: (1) d1a5b7cb10 attributes the bug's squash only to its huge change of motion; adding that the bug is soft and the glass strong would make it airtight. (2) 78962112bf's 'Floats up, since the air inside is light' was checked as the brief asked: it is wrong by its reason, since a breath-filled balloon does not float. Grade notes spot-checked: TEKS 6.7C ('simultaneous force pairs'), TEKS 5.7B ('a balloon rocket on a string') and Florida SC.5.P.13.3 are quoted correctly. Physics Classroom pages returned 403, so its bug-and-bus wording was read from search snippets only.
